title: Reject stale-generation mutations with an attempt fencing guard
description:
Objective: make a late call from a superseded execution fail instead of corrupting current state. Today packages/moe-daemon/src/util/enforcement.ts guards ownership by comparing worker ids and keeps legacy tolerances for an omitted id or an unassigned task, so nothing distinguishes a live worker from a zombie that woke up after reassignment.

Deliverable: an assertAttemptCurrent guard in util/enforcement.ts that takes the caller's attempt id or generation and the task, and throws a named MoeError when the attempt is not the current one for that task. It sits alongside the existing assertWorkerOwns rather than replacing it, and the existing omitted-id tolerance stays intact for callers that predate attempts.

Not in scope: calling the guard from any tool handler. Wiring is the sibling attempt-lifecycle task; this task lands the guard and its tests so the wiring task stays small.

Depends on the ExecutionAttempt store because the guard reads the current generation from it.

Verification: npx vitest run src/util/enforcement.test.ts from packages/moe-daemon.
definitionOfDone: assertAttemptCurrent is exported from packages/moe-daemon/src/util/enforcement.ts and reads the current attempt through the attempt store
A call carrying generation N against a task whose current attempt is generation N+1 throws a named error code, asserted exactly
A call carrying the current generation passes, and a call from a caller that supplies no attempt identity keeps the existing legacy tolerance rather than throwing
New cases in src/util/enforcement.test.ts cover current, stale and absent attempt identity
npx vitest run src/util/enforcement.test.ts passes and npm test in packages/moe-daemon stays green
taskRails: Add the guard beside assertWorkerOwns; do not change or weaken the existing ownership guards.
No tool handler is edited in this task.

implementationPlan.description: RED FIRST. Add the new cases to packages/moe-daemon/src/util/enforcement.test.ts, preserving every existing test unchanged. They will not compile until the next step adds the export, so write them against the intended signature and treat the compile failure as the starting point rather than as the red evidence - the meaningful red comes from the mutation proofs in step 4. Cases, each asserting exact values: a caller carrying generation N against a task whose current attempt is generation N+1 throws, and the assertion checks BOTH the numeric error code and the exact codeName string, because several codes share a number in this codebase and a name-only or number-only assertion proves little. A caller carrying the current generation passes. A caller carrying a generation HIGHER than the current one also throws - a caller from the future is as wrong as one from the past, and this case is what kills a less-than comparison masquerading as a correct implementation. A caller supplying the current attempt id passes; a different attempt id throws. A caller supplying both an id and a generation that disagree with each other throws without consulting anything else. A caller supplying no attempt identity at all keeps the existing legacy tolerance and does not throw, which the Definition of Done requires explicitly. A task with no attempt record at all keeps that tolerance too, even when the caller supplies an identity - see the reasoning in the next step. Malformed identity is refused rather than coerced: a generation that is null, a string, a boolean, fractional, negative or outside the safe-integer range raises the invalid-input error, never a silent pass and never a fall-through to the legacy branch. Finally, one control proving the rails held: the existing ownership and context guards behave exactly as before, including their own omitted-worker tolerance.

Cases added (26 `it` blocks, 41 assertions-as-tests once it.each expands):
- generation: N behind current (throws, asserts currentGeneration 2 / callerGeneration 1), current (passes), N AHEAD of current (throws — this is the case that kills a `<` comparison).
- attempt id: current passes; superseded id throws; an id absent from the store throws.
- both fields: matching pair passes; id-current+generation-stale throws; generation-current+id-stale throws. Those two kill an OR implementation — a self-inconsistent pair can never pass because BOTH fields are compared against the current attempt, so no separate cross-check is needed.
- legacy tolerance: identity argument `undefined`; `{}`; `{attemptId: undefined, generation: undefined}`; task with NO attempt record at all even when an identity IS supplied; and a store holding only OTHER tasks' attempts.
- task scoping: another task's live generation (7) does NOT satisfy this task's fence — kills a store lookup that forgets to filter by taskId.
- all-closed: attempts exist but every one is `closed` -> throws, and asserts `currentAttemptId`/`currentGeneration` are null. This is the distinction step 1 flagged: `currentAttempt()` returns null for BOTH "no record" and "all closed", so the tolerance keys on `listAttempts(state, taskId).length === 0` and a closed-out caller is correctly treated as a zombie.
- malformed generation (9 values x 2 contexts = 18 cases): null, '2', true, 1.5, -1, 0, MAX_SAFE_INTEGER+1, NaN, Infinity -> INVALID_INPUT, asserted both with a populated store AND with an EMPTY store. The empty-store half is the important one: 0 and '' are falsy, so a `!identity.generation` check would silently fall through to the legacy tolerance instead of refusing.
- malformed attemptId (4 cases): null, '', '   ', 42 -> INVALID_INPUT. Plus a non-object identity argument.
- error hygiene: context keys are exactly [callerAttemptId, callerGeneration, currentAttemptId, currentGeneration, taskId] — nothing else leaks; message contains `moe.complete_step` when a tool name is passed.
- RAILS CONTROL (new `describe`, 5 tests): assertWorkerOwns still tolerates an omitted workerId on a claimed task, still throws NOT_ALLOWED with owner/caller context on a mismatch, still no-ops on an unassigned task; assertContextFetched still tolerates an omitted workerId and still throws NOT_ALLOWED for an un-fetched owner.

implementationPlan.description: IMPLEMENT THE GUARD BESIDE THE OTHERS. Add assertAttemptCurrent to packages/moe-daemon/src/util/enforcement.ts, placed next to assertWorkerOwns and leaving every existing guard untouched - a task rail. Signature takes the StateManager, the Task, the caller's attempt identity as an optional object holding an optional attempt id and an optional generation, and the usual optional tool name for the message. Order of decisions, and each of them is deliberate. First, no identity supplied - the argument absent, or present with neither field - returns immediately under the same legacy tolerance the module already grants an omitted worker id, warning the same way; callers that predate attempts must keep working. Second, validate any supplied generation before using it: a non-negative safe integer or nothing, refusing anything else as invalid input with no coercion, matching how the plan-revision work handled untrusted revision tokens. Third, read the current attempt from the store using the API recorded in step 1. If the task has NO attempt record at all, return under the legacy tolerance even though an identity was supplied - a task that never opened an attempt cannot have superseded anybody, and refusing here would break every task that predates the rollout the moment the sibling wiring task starts calling this guard. Log it so the case is visible. Fourth, compare: a supplied attempt id must equal the current attempt's id, and a supplied generation must EQUAL the current generation - not be less than it - so both a stale and an impossible future caller are refused by the same expression. When both fields are supplied they must also agree with each other. Any mismatch throws a MoeError carrying a stable codeName of ATTEMPT_SUPERSEDED over the existing state-conflict numeric code, with context limited to the task id, the current attempt id and generation, and what the caller presented. Use the state-conflict code rather than the not-allowed code the ownership guard uses, because a superseded attempt is a state race, not a permission failure - and record that choice in a comment so a later reader does not 'fix' it. Error handling note for the header comment: this guard fences DAEMON mutations only. It cannot stop a superseded CLI from writing files in a shared workspace, which the epic notes state explicitly, so the comment must not imply it prevents that.

File keeps its CRLF working-tree endings (core.autocrlf=true normalizes on commit).

Exports added: `interface AttemptIdentity { attemptId?: string; generation?: number }` and `assertAttemptCurrent(state: StateManager, task: Task, identity: AttemptIdentity | undefined, toolName = 'unknown'): void` (42-line body, under the 50 bar). Private helpers: `firstAttemptNotice(key)` (bounded once-per-key gate sharing warnMissingWorkerId's existing map and cap with its own key prefixes; warnMissingWorkerId itself is NOT edited), `validateAttemptIdentity`, `describeAttempt`.

Decision order as implemented:
1. Identity absent (undefined, JSON null, `{}`, or both fields undefined) -> return. Warns once per (task, tool) ONLY when the task is claimed, mirroring assertContextFetched's `if (task.assignedWorkerId) warnMissingWorkerId(...)`, so plugin/human board actions on unclaimed tasks will not spam once handlers are wired.
2. Non-object identity -> INVALID_INPUT. Supplied fields validated with `!== undefined` (not truthiness), so `generation: 0` and `attemptId: ''` are refused rather than falling into step 1. Generation must be a safe integer in [1, MAX_ATTEMPT_GENERATION].
3. `listAttempts(state, task.id).length === 0` -> return with a once-per-(task, tool) `logger.info` line. Documented as DO NOT "FIX" INTO A REFUSAL.
4. `currentAttempt(state, task.id)`; each supplied field must be `===` to the current attempt's. All-closed means current is null, so any identity is refused.
Mismatch -> `new MoeError(MoeErrorCode.STATE_CONFLICT, ..., { taskId, currentAttemptId, currentGeneration, callerAttemptId, callerGeneration }, 'ATTEMPT_SUPERSEDED')`.

Two deliberate choices beyond the plan's literal text:
- (a) Plan said "a non-negative safe integer". I implemented POSITIVE, so 0 is refused. schema.ts documents generations as starting at 1, and attemptStore's decodeStoredGeneration already refuses a stored value below 1. Generation 0 can never be current, and refusing it as input also closes the falsy fall-through.
- (b) No unassigned-task early return. assertWorkerOwns has one for the plugin/human path, but those callers present no identity and are already covered by step 1. A caller presenting an identity is an attempt-aware worker. An early return there would let a zombie through exactly when its task has been released. Documented in the doc comment.

The header comment states that the guard fences DAEMON MUTATIONS ONLY and that a superseded CLI can still write to a shared workspace. It also records why the guard raises STATE_CONFLICT and not NOT_ALLOWED.

Added one pinning test during implementation: identity argument JSON `null` is treated as absent. This grants nothing a caller could not already get by omitting the field.

implementationPlan.note:
ADVERSARIAL REVIEW. I read the full diff as an attacker. It turned up 3 real defects, each fixed test-first (red, then green), and each fix is now covered by a new mutation.

FIXED:
1. DEDUPE MAP COUPLING. This was a subtle rail breach. The attempt notices shared warnMissingWorkerId's bounded 1000-entry FIFO map, so a flood of attempt notices evicted the ownership guard's entries and made assertWorkerOwns warn a second time. That is an existing guard changing behaviour. Fix: a separate `attemptNoticed` map with the same cap constant. RED test `existing guards are unchanged by the attempt fence > attempt-fence notices never evict the ownership guard warning dedupe` failed with "expected LOG to be called +0 times, but got 1 times". Mutation M9, which points the gate back at the shared map, turns it red again.
2. REFUSAL RENDERING COULD CRASH. `String(Object.create(null))` and `JSON.stringify(10n)` both throw a raw TypeError, which would have surfaced as an internal error instead of INVALID_INPUT. A 10k-character generation string was also echoed in full. Fix: `renderUntrusted(value)`, which never calls String() on object, function or symbol values and truncates to 40 chars. RED `refuses unrenderable values as invalid input rather than crashing` failed with "TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value". RED `bounds how much of a refused value it echoes back` failed with "expected 10090 to be less than 300". Mutation M10 turns both red.
3. HEADER / MESSAGE WORDING. The header now says the guard stops a zombie from getting a DAEMON mutation recorded, and that it is inert until a tool handler calls it. The SCOPE paragraph keeps the "cannot stop a superseded CLI writing to a shared workspace" caveat, unsoftened. The error message now reads `Superseded attempt refused by moe.<tool> on task <id>: caller presented <id|generation>, current attempt is <id (generation N)|none (all closed)>`.

CHECKLIST ANSWERS:
- Omitting a field: whichever field is presented is compared. Omitting both gives the legacy tolerance, which the DoD requires. THEORETICAL: generations are predictable (+1), so a caller that FORGES the next generation passes a generation-only check. Fencing tokens are not authentication. The sibling should pass the attempt id, which is a 128-bit random id, whenever it has it.
- Numeric-string generation: refused as INVALID_INPUT, proven by M4.
- Missing record: this is a deliberate, documented tolerance, proven by M3. attemptStore has no delete API, so records vanishing is reachable only by hand-editing .moe/, which is forbidden. All-closed is REFUSED, and a test covers that.
- Equality: `===` on both fields. M1 (ordering) and M5 (OR) are both red.
- Existing guards: 0 removed lines in enforcement.ts. The 5 rails-control tests pass, and M9 guards the dedupe.
- Type-only import: `import type { StateManager }` at line 4. The full suite shows no cycle. The runtime chain enforcement -> attemptStore -> errors/ids is acyclic.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered: Extending assertWorkerOwns to also consider the attempt - rejected by a task rail and on its own merits: the existing guard is called by many handlers with a worker id and no attempt identity, and widening it would change behaviour for all of them. Refusing when a task has no attempt record even though the caller supplied an identity - rejected: the sibling wiring task will meet tasks that predate the rollout, and a guard that refuses those would either break them or force that task to grow special cases, defeating the purpose of landing the guard separately. Comparing with less-than so only older generations are refused - rejected and explicitly tested against: a caller claiming a generation beyond the current one is just as wrong, and equality is the expression that catches both. Making the caller pass the attempt record itself rather than an identity - rejected: the whole point is that a superseded caller holds a stale token, so the guard must resolve the current truth from the store rather than trust what it was handed. Coercing a numeric string generation - rejected: untrusted identity is validated, never coerced, consistent with the revision-token handling already shipped.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights: Measured live on 2026-09-11. enforcement.ts is small and uniform: every guard today is a pure function over a Task with no state dependency, and each one grants the same two legacy tolerances - return early when the task is unassigned, and return after a deprecation warning when the caller omits its worker id. The new guard is the first in this module to need the state handle, which is why the StateManager import must be type-only: erased at compile time, so no runtime cycle can form between the enforcement helpers and the state layer. The prerequisite store is in flight rather than landed, and its exported names are not settled - the plan for that task proposed a currentAttempt helper, but the guard must bind to whatever actually shipped, which is why step 1 records the real API before anything is written. The error-code choice is a judgement worth stating: assertWorkerOwns raises the not-allowed code because a wrong owner is a permission problem, whereas a superseded attempt is a state race, so this guard uses the state-conflict code with a stable ATTEMPT_SUPERSEDED name, matching how the plan-revision compare-and-swap named its mismatch. Several codes share a number in this codebase, so every test assertion must check the number AND the name.
planningNotes.risks: The prerequisite is not landed, so step 1 must block rather than guess its API; binding to proposed names that did not ship is the single likeliest way this task wastes a worker's session. The no-attempt-record tolerance is the second hazard - it looks like a hole and will tempt a reviewer or a later editor to remove it, so it needs a comment explaining that removing it breaks every task predating the rollout, plus a test that fails when it goes. Use equality, not an ordering comparison. Keep the StateManager import type-only or risk a runtime import cycle that will surface as a confusing suite-wide failure. Do not touch any existing guard or any tool handler - both are task rails, and the whole reason this guard lands alone is to keep the wiring task small. Finally, do not let the header comment overclaim: the epic notes are explicit that a generation fences daemon mutations only and cannot stop a superseded external process from writing to a shared workspace, and that caveat must not be softened here, because later slices will inherit whatever this comment says.
